title: How GPS Knows Where You Are

sentences.text: Many people worry that a global satellite network is constantly tracking the live location of their mobile phone.
You might wonder how your phone determines your exact position on Earth using signals from space without ever sending any data back.
It is a satellite-based navigation system that provides geolocation and time information to a receiver anywhere near the Earth.
The entire network does not require you to transmit any data to function.
Your device operates completely independently of any telephone or internet reception.
To understand how this passive network works, you need to look at the space segment of the system.
The space segment is composed of 24 to 32 space vehicles orbiting in medium Earth orbit.
These satellites orbit at an altitude of approximately 20,200 kilometres.
Each vehicle makes two complete orbits each sidereal day, which is about 11 hours and 58 minutes.
The satellites broadcast these vital data points continuously down to the surface of the planet.
How do those radio waves turn into a measurement of distance on your device?
The time delay between when a satellite transmits a signal and when a receiver gets it is proportional to the distance.
Modern electronics can measure this signal offset to within about 10 nanoseconds for the civilian code.
Once your device calculates the distance to a satellite, it uses that data to narrow down where you could be.
If you know you are a certain distance from a single satellite, you could be anywhere on a sphere surrounding it.
Adding a second satellite narrows your possible location down to the circle where two spheres intersect.
Bringing in a third satellite shrinks the intersection down to just two points in three-dimensional space.
One of those two points is usually out in space, leaving only a single realistic position on the Earth.
There is a major catch in this simple geometry that requires an extra step from your receiver.
That cheap clock has a time offset relative to the true time kept by the satellite network.
Because of this offset, your device cannot measure true ranges and instead calculates pseudo-ranges.
To solve for this extra unknown variable, your receiver must look at more than just three space vehicles.
Even with four satellites and good geometry, tiny invisible physics forces threaten to ruin the accuracy of your navigation.
General relativity also shows that clocks located deeper in a gravitational well tick slower.
Because the satellites are far above the Earth, their clocks run faster by about 45,850 nanoseconds per day due to gravity.
Combined, these relativistic effects cause satellite clocks to gain about 38.6 microseconds every single day.
Without corrections, errors of roughly 11.4 km per day would accumulate in the position.
Engineers solve this by giving the atomic clocks on board a rate offset prior to launch to keep them perfectly synced.
So how does GPS know where you are without ever tracking you?
Your phone simply listens to passive radio signals broadcast by an overhead constellation of ultra-precise floating atomic clocks.
By measuring the time delay of signals from four separate satellites, your device calculates its exact position locally.
No data travels back to space, leaving your location entirely private while guiding you precisely across the world.
